prompt: You keep a sine wave’s frequency in hertz fixed and double the sample rate. What happens to its progress through a cycle between neighbouring samples?

options.explanation: More frequent samples leave less time for the wave to progress, rather than more.

options.text: It stays the same because the wave frequency is unchanged
options.explanation: The physical frequency is unchanged, but each sample gap is shorter, so cycles per sample changes.
Correct. Twice as many sampling intervals fit into the same cycle, so each advances only half as far.

workedExample:
1. Holding hertz fixed keeps each complete cycle the same length in seconds.
2. Doubling sample rate puts twice as many equal gaps within it.
3. Each gap therefore covers half the previous fraction of a cycle.

link.title: Primary source: The Scientist and Engineer’s Guide to DSP

prompt: A unit-amplitude sine starts at zero phase. You change only its starting phase to a quarter turn. What happens to its first sample?

options.text: It changes from zero to positive one
options.explanation: Correct. Sine of a quarter turn is one.
Phase controls the starting point, so the initial value can change.
A constant phase change does not change the angle advance per sample.

workedExample:
1. Zero-phase sine starts at its centre and rises.
2. Advancing its starting position by a quarter turn puts it at the positive maximum.
3. Amplitude and frequency stay unchanged because only starting phase changed.

link.title: Primary source: The Scientist and Engineer’s Guide to DSP

prompt: A finite sampled sine has an ideal amplitude of 1. Which statements hold? Select all that apply.

options.text: Its largest recorded sample must be exactly 1
options.explanation: Sampling may miss the instant of the ideal maximum.

options.text: Its recorded sample magnitudes cannot exceed 1 in exact arithmetic
options.explanation: Correct. Sine stays between negative one and one.

options.text: For a known nonzero frequency in cycles per sample, changing only the sample rate changes its interpreted hertz value
options.explanation: Correct. A fixed nonzero cycles-per-sample frequency scales with sample rate. This does not claim that a finite sample sequence uniquely identifies its original continuous frequency.

workedExample:
1. The ideal amplitude bounds the exact sine values.
2. A finite sampling grid need not contain a maximum.
3. Physical frequency requires both the sequence and its sample rate.

link.title: Primary source: The Scientist and Engineer’s Guide to DSP
